notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00519.opp-gr: 1.4: an apparatus line ('P = Codex Parisinus gr. 2998, Ath = Athous Laurae Ω 123') has intruded into the text and is omitted; 'ὧς ἴ’ τι' is corrupt, read as 'even if they had caused some grief'. 7.1: 'ροῦ χαλεπότης' is mutilated, probably 'καιροῦ' ('harshness of circumstance'); the construction 'τοῦ μηδὲν ἀνάξιον ὑπομεῖναι δόξης' is awkward. 9.1: stray numeral '5' omitted. 9.2 (sect. 10): text lacunose after 'ἐγὼ <δὲ> παρ’ ὑμῶν'; what Demosthenes asks is lost. 12.1: 'ἱστᾶι' read as 'ἔσται'. 14.1: 'ὦ ἄνδρες δικασταί' (jurors) is odd in an assembly speech but translated as given.

16.1: 'μικρὸν τὸ κακὸν τῆς ὑμετέρας ἐρρωμένης τάξεως' is obscure and possibly corrupt; rendered as a comparison. 21 (20.2): the final sentence ('τίς ξένους, τίς συμμάχους αὐτοὺς γράψοντας εἷναι χρείαν· αἰτίαν, ἂν καθαρεύητε, σχῆτε') is corrupt, with text apparently lost; translated as fragments. 22.1: 'as once long ago [he gave] the cost of a chorus' presumably alludes to Demosthenes' voluntary choregia; the subject is uncertain. 22.3: the bracketed '[ναί]', deleted by the edition, is left untranslated. 28.2: the clause 'τὸ μὲν ἐμὸν μέρος ἐστὲ μὲν ἐπὶ Θρᾴκης [Χαλκίδος] σώζονται δὲ Φωκεῦσιν αἱ πόλεις' is corrupt; the sense is conjectural. 30.1: the question about Python ('θυμὸν πολὺν ἀντιφέροντι πρὸς τὸ πῦρ σὺν ἠγώνισμαι') is corrupt; historically Demosthenes opposed Python, so 'contended against' may be meant.

33: the text is defective at the start ('<θῶ> ... σθαί'); read as θῶ φείσεσθαι/σώσεσθαι, 'suppose that he will spare me'. A stray bracket after ἔστω δὲ and the letters 'RIV' in 43 are omitted as printing debris. 37: 'τὸν δὲ τῷ ἐνταῦθ’ ἀρκέσαι πρὸς ἐκεῖνον' is obscure and possibly corrupt; the rendering is tentative. 'Hand over' renders ἐκδίδοσθαι/ἔκδοσις (surrender of a person). 'Sycophant' here means a malicious accuser.

nodes.text: XIX.
After the events at Chaeronea Philip demanded Demosthenes [be handed over]. The people asked for five days for consideration. During these Demosthenes asks to be allowed to die.
Demosthenes.

In vain, men of Athens, did you ask for these five days from those who have come from Macedonia, as though you would make some better decision in them about my person. For I am cutting short this long time for you, so that you may not owe the ambassadors of Philip any gratitude even for this, and I am giving the answer on your behalf in deed. I ask you, men of Athens, to give me a share of the hemlock, and to send the ambassadors away carrying the message most pleasing to their master: that Demosthenes is dead.

2. What I expected, you most humane of all men, you have done: on hearing of my death you were downcast. For such is your people: it pities the unfortunate, even if they have caused it some grief before, let alone those who have shown unbroken goodwill towards the people. But I, apart from my other reasons, think I ought to die because of this very pity you now feel at what I have said. For it is far better for the people to weep over me as I die here than as I am dragged off by the ambassadors to the enemy, to my disgrace and yours. For if you cannot bear even this more moderate [fate], since to obtain burial at home is no small consolation, how will you bear that most pitiable of all things?

3. Let none of you, if tears come to my words while I am speaking, think that this has happened to me because I cling to life and fear death. For anything, men of Athens, even the most terrible thing, is light to me if I must suffer it for you. But ever since that day on which the divine power judged the battle badly, I have not ceased lamenting night or day, admiring the courage of those who stood in the battle line and blaming fortune. And now I have come straight from tears and from deliberating on behalf of the unfortunate. For I was considering, be well assured, what remedy there might be for what has happened. It is no wonder, then, if on remembering Chaeronea I should feel something of the kind.

4. When I first heard that an embassy had arrived from Macedonia, some such reasoning as this occurred to me: that Philip, being a man not altogether without sense, does not trust what has been achieved, and has probably said to himself something like this: 'I, the son of Amyntas who paid tribute to the Athenians, and barely saved by the humanity of Iphicrates, their general, small and lowly as I was and afraid of the barbarians around me, and expecting to do the Athenians harm [only] with the Thebans, but without them to suffer no small harm, have now defeated the Athenians and Thebans together, though beaten in the first battle and beaten in the second, and having enjoyed fortune only in the third.

What then does a man of sense do? Not consider the alliance of this [goddess] secure, whose business it is to leap across from the victors to the vanquished, and to raise up and pull down the same people. For there is a fear that those I now hold as captives I may see, a little later, holding Macedonia.'

For he had heard, men of Athens, about our city, and it has not escaped him that no setback has ever brought it down completely, but it has sprung back from those very reverses. He had often heard of Amphipolis and the dead there; he had heard of Delium and those who fell there; greatest of all, he had heard of Sicily and the tens of thousands; he had heard of the Hellespont itself and the Thirty Tyrants, after whom came Cnidus and a sea battle and once more the walls of Conon. I supposed that, having learned and remembered these things, he wanted to lock in his good fortune with friendship and did not wish to expose what he had achieved to a second trial, and that the ambassadors had come to discuss some agreement with us.

But when someone came up to me and said that the men from there had come to take away one of the Athenians, 'Not while I am alive,' I said. 'For I will come forward and read out the laws of Solon, which judge an Athenian at Athens and do not hand him over untried to the lawlessness of tyrants; and I will speak about the character of the city: that this people, surely, was not brought down by the harshness of [circumstance], nor the strength of the Thebans, nor the might of the Lacedaemonians, nor the barbarian's army that set everything in motion, sailing through land and marching across the sea that it had bound, and driving the Athenians out of both city and land, so as to submit to anything unworthy of their glory. And this was well known to this man's ancestor Alexander, who was so far from taking anything from you that, though he brought the great gifts of the King, he barely escaped with his life.'

With such words and many others I was planning to speak in support of the man in danger, for I, fool that I was, thought the evil was heading for someone else. And yet as soon as I heard, I ought to have expected that what they had come in search of was myself. For there were many things that created this expectation: a war between an orator and a tyrant, long and painful speeches, decrees fighting against his plots, many embassies, gold disdained, trials of those who had taken it, public speeches rousing a sluggish people.

How then would he have come for someone else and not me? Why say much? The ambassadors said to you: 'We have come, men of Athens, to receive from you Demosthenes, the enemy of Philip. Hand him over.' On hearing this I bid farewell to the words with which I would have saved another, plentiful as they were, thinking it vulgar to speak on my own behalf, and I sat in silence waiting for what the people would decide, thinking it possible to give an answer befitting free men. What then did you do? O Chaeronea, wretched place, how you have thrown into confusion a people noble and able to bear misfortunes! The present events too belonged to the misfortune there. You asked for five days for deliberation. And the Macedonians, reluctantly, but they agreed.

10. But, most excellent of ambassadors, there is no need for delay, nor does the people need such a favour. I do not allow them to waste so much time. Today, as far as my part is concerned, go back. For these men asked five days of you, but I [...] of you. There is a law among us that one who does not wish to live may die, which Philip has not yet abolished. So while it is in force, I will enjoy its help.

'Recourse to the law,' someone says, 'is for those who suffer from some incurable disease, and for those who have lost children or property or suffered some other such thing. But if the people needs longer deliberation about you, how does this deserve death?' Let someone say this, men of Athens, to private persons, whose fortunes are judged by their private affairs. But an orator, and this Demosthenes, the emulator of Aristides and Nicias and Pericles, do not examine with an eye to his body and property.

For I have not spent my life caring for these things or praying to the gods for them, but that the perjured Philip might perish, which will surely happen even if Demosthenes dies, and that the people of the Athenians might be raised on high by battles and victories and trophies no less than those wonderful ones of which one stands in our land at Marathon, another at Plataea, and others in these nearby islands, Euboea and Salamis.

These things I prayed for, these I longed for, and to see you heirs of your ancestors' spirit. The choice was noble, and equal to that of those who ran to Marathon: you too ran to the borders of Boeotia for the common freedom of the Greeks; some of you fell like the famous Cynegirus, like Callimachus, like those who filled the tomb there. But what has happened in this assembly is petty and abject and unworthy of that expedition.

For we have met with misfortune, I admit. What wonder then if I cannot bear seeing in misfortune those I wished to prosper? In the Attic assembly, O Zeus, the Athenians begged the Macedonians not to [require them to] give a quick answer. In these few words, gentlemen of the jury, in which you postponed that answer, you advised Demosthenes to die. I saw the people that frightened Greeks and barbarians humbled, the opposite of what I prayed for. O Earth and Sun, I have failed in a great and noble endeavour. I cannot live while you hold assemblies like this.

Many men have often killed themselves over their beloveds. I too see my beloved, the people of the Athenians, no longer blooming as before. So, that I may be spared from seeing such assemblies, I depart today, setting a fine end to my political career.

You say: I have not had my eyes knocked out. Would that I had suffered this while you were great. I have not had my leg cut off. Would that I had lost both, if it meant that you were kept safe. My body is not wasting away. That is a small evil, set against the strength of your ranks. You see that even Philip does not shrink from such a contribution, but buys glory with parts of his body.

I wish the god had given an oracle that Philip would perish if Demosthenes gave up his daughter for the city. For then you would not have seen me looking for poison, but imitating Erechtheus. But as things are, as I have often told you, I cannot bear it, and at the same time I am considering how I might benefit you even in the present situation. For my death, like my life, must become a gain to the city. How then will this be? Consider.

18. You have now asked for five days for deliberation. So in these you will either hand [me] over or not. If, then, you hand me over, and they take me away with your consent, you will break many laws, men of Athens, and you will show yourselves strangers to your fathers, and you will teach Philip to look for another after me, and after him yet another, and all of my rank in turn, until the speaker's platform belongs only to those who speak on his behalf; and they will easily move that the triremes sail for Philip, that soldiers follow him, and that your general go with him.

These are the great harms; another is that you will be slandered before all mankind as people who do not properly repay kindness to those who are loyal to you. And it is no small misfortune in the present circumstances that the people is so very well known. For because of your many embassies, men of Athens, you have become known not only among the Greeks but also to not a few of the barbarians.

If you were to send embassies to them, calling on them [to march] against Philip (for it will come, the right moment for this too will come), do you not think they will all at once say: 'You are a fine lot to talk of friendship with us! You handed over Demosthenes, a sleepless and hard-working orator who always got the better of Philip's ambassadors among us, to your enemies, without fearing the gods, without feeling shame before men, or before the very platform among you from which he delivered those many fine speeches. What then should we expect from you? Shall we fight alongside you, men who do not know how to remember a kindness?'

21. Do you see how my being handed over by you to the Macedonians shuts the cities against you? It also makes the best of those in public life, men of Athens, speechless. For who will stand up when the herald calls? Who will make speeches that are to your advantage but to his own loss? Who will find sources of money? Who mercenaries, who allies, ... need; ... you may incur blame, if you keep yourselves clean.

For this reason I am shifting the reproach from you onto myself; or rather, I am freeing you from reproach and winning undying glory for myself by not allowing you to do any wrong. For do not let Philip be able to say this, whether in jest or in earnest, whether to those who come to him or to the Greeks through ambassadors: 'The Athenians handed over their popular leader to me.' I do not want that man to have such words at his disposal. For if even now, by slandering the city, he has won over not a few, what will he be when his accusations are true? Let it be said throughout the inhabited world: 'He gave himself up for the common glory; as Leos [gave] his daughters, as Codrus himself, as once long ago [he gave] the cost of a chorus, so Demosthenes gave his life.'

23. Very well. If I am handed over by you, men of Athens, so many evils and still more will surround the city; but if, on deliberation, you decide to refuse Philip and to fear what is just more than the defeat that has befallen [us], then this very thing in turn is reason enough for me to die: that I should have to wait for so long a deliberation. For what do you need these five days for? Tell me. So that you may learn from so-and-so whether this Demosthenes here is useful and deserves to be saved by the Athenians? And why do I live, if after so long a political career I am unknown? It cannot be. I prevent wretched assemblies by a noble death. I will not give grounds for the charge that the people of the Athenians, the quickest of all at finding what is needed, spent five days on matters so obvious.

24. Consider further what the business will be like. You will fill the assembly every day, and those of Philip's party will come forward and say 'the warmonger', 'the man who throws the city into confusion', and things like that, and will urge you to hand [me] over. Then will the democrats not shout at this: 'You lie. Did Demosthenes break the peace? By doing what? [By defending] the Chersonese, Perinthus, Byzantium, the grain convoys, by preventing the Peloponnese from being undermined, by blaming the man who was plundering the ships? Ought he to have let it go? A wonderful peace indeed, that he should seize the city's possessions while the city keeps to the treaty! No one breaks a peace by defending himself; the one who breaks it is the man who does the things that will make others defend themselves.'

With such a defence, and after that carrying many of my decrees in their hands instead of suppliant branches, they will read out the ones under which ambassadors went out, under which triremes sailed, under which you were not driven out of some places and recovered others. These things, men of Athens, every day, these five times over, these as long as the ambassadors allow. And in addition to these, the lament of my fellow demesmen, the tears of my fellow tribesmen, of my household, of my relatives, of those I ransomed from Macedonia, for whom I made their debt a gift. They will even bring my daughter to the assemblies to beg you: 'Save my father, have pity on him.'

What then will the people do? It will bend, and will do for me what our ancestors did for Adrastus and for Oedipus the Theban, and, as in Euripides' play, for the children of Heracles, and, as in Phrynichus', for Miletus; and it will answer the ambassadors, shouting and weeping at once: 'We do not hand over Demosthenes. We have not yet fallen, we have not yet suffered anything so great. We were defeated, but perhaps we shall win. He will take Demosthenes when he takes the city.'

If in this way, men of Athens, I am saved, with my friends begging and you pitying, what life will be left to me? What shall I spend it doing? Shall I sit idle, listening to others speak, after so long a political career, men of Athens? And is that fine for you? Or shall I again say and propose those familiar things: 'Let us march out, let us pay the war-tax, let us warn the Greeks, let us fight the defeat over again, let us hold on to our empire. You are heirs of this noble thing'?

And who among those I have offended, whom I annoy by speaking, will not rise up insolently and throw me off the platform: 'The man who was surrendered, the disgraced man, the man saved by pity, the slave of those who wept for him: must this man climb onto the platform and be prouder than he should? Are you bold again? You seem to want a second dose of misfortune.' Do not keep me alive, men of Athens, for such words, but while you still stand on your former glory, put me to death.

29. 'And how,' someone says, 'is it not madness to want to die now, when it is possible to wait for Philip's decision, if indeed he takes [you]? Perhaps he will spare you when he takes you, such great kindness has he shown to many.' Will Philip spare Demosthenes? Will he not kill him? And remembering what? The speeches on behalf of the Olynthians? Which? The first, or the second, or the third? Or rather those on behalf of the Phocians, some of which the people heard, others the law court? By which he knows that, as far as my part goes, you are [still] in Thrace [Chalcidice] and the cities of the Phocians are kept safe; and because of these splendid [speeches] Philip will not put up with being wronged.

These things first provoke the man. Then, as for the things for which I never stopped exposing him, the mercenaries, the foot companions, about which I hold the same opinion even if they have won, do I think I have found in them reasons why he will spare me? Did I contend alongside Python as he poured out his words and brought great passion against the fire? Did I abolish the navy by a wicked law? When Elatea was seized, did I praise keeping quiet?

Do you not think, men of Athens, that for each of these I owe him my death? Do you not think he has often said to himself: 'Shall I take the man who calls me a barbarian, who reviles Pella, who by his speeches overcame my kindnesses to the Thebans? I freed them from war, but Demosthenes brought the city against me, and because of this Chaeronea received the battle instead of Eleusis.'

32. What then? Will he take me and crown me and invite me to dinner? Of course, so little has he suffered! For will he not offer victory sacrifices when he has Demosthenes? Will he not be prouder of this than of his good fortune in the battle? Will he not gather the traitors, Daochus, Hieronymus, Mnaseas, Euxitheus? Demades, of course, will see me being led away, but will he not send word to those others: 'Come and look at the incorruptible man, the one who could not be taken. He has been taken and become mine, not from the battle line but from the assembly. Stand round him, strike him, beat him, flog him, divide up his limbs, taste his flesh. This man used to call you, my friends, wretches. Tear apart the fortunate man, you wretches!'

33. Do you want me to suppose, men of Athens, that the man will spare me, an impossible thing? Let it be so; let it be granted. Do you want me to suppose that I will even receive honours from him? Let this too be granted. And what would become of me through Philip's kindness, when, having power to kill me, he lets me live after heaping many reproaches on me? Hemlock is not more frightening to me than his friendship. For if he were to imitate what the King did for Themistocles, giving me much land around Bolbe, or all of Mygdonia, or the whole of Anthemus, the bait for the wretched Olynthians, could I bear to live in Macedonia, among its customs and laws, after those of Draco, O gods, and of Solon, under tyranny after democracy, among the licentious and the drunk, among mime-actors and bad dancers, mocked and jeered at: 'This is Demosthenes the bad-tempered, the difficult, the water-drinker, the one who ridiculed our good living'?

I would rather accept being cut and burned every day than join Philip in speaking for honours to Parmenion. And what if he orders me to go as an envoy to the cities and sing a recantation, that what I used to tell you before was a sycophant's talk, but this comes from the truth: 'Philip is a descendant of Zeus himself, good in character, irresistible in power, just towards his friends, attentive to the gods'? Will Demosthenes utter these words among the Argives and the Messenians and the other Greeks?

35. May I never be saved at your expense, men of Athens, and may I never value my life so highly that from longing to live I harm the city that bore me. And I would harm it if such a decree prevailed among you. But it will not prevail, as long as there is hemlock, nor will anyone write at Athens: 'Resolved by the Council and the people of the Athenians that Demosthenes of Paeania be handed over to Philip the Macedonian to treat as he wishes.' May the Metroön never receive such writings, and may no others contrary to them be mixed in with what Hyperides and Demomeles have written about me; for it is shameful, shameful, that in the same city the same man should now be crowned for his excellence and a little later be handed over to his enemies. Rather, let the last decree agree with the earlier ones: 'Demosthenes was crowned by the Athenians.' Let this stand, and let someone grind the poison.

36. 'But Philip will be angry,' one of those grown rich from him will say, 'if I die like this. For he wants to become master of my life himself.' That would be more pleasant for Philip, I know it myself, but this too is no small thing. For even if I had happened to die of illness, it would have been a great thing for him. And now he desires to take me and cut me to pieces, but he will also be pleased to learn I am dead. For he does not so much want to exact punishment for the past as to be rid of my statesmanship for the time to come. For these are the three things, men of Athens, that Philip fears most: the gods' oracles on behalf of the city, your inborn courage in the face of dangers, and my frankness on the speaker's platform. For he hears the oracles singing that the city is a wineskin that cannot be sunk, he has come to know your natures in those who fell nobly, and he knows that my zeal does not give way in a hard time.

So he wants me dead, so that you may not have, besides your courage and your fortune, the third thing, Demosthenes' goodwill, since he hears on the one hand that Themistocles by his judgement overcame that great power of the Mede, and on the other that Conon, an exile, drove the Spartans from the sea. Well then, what he sought most, this he will have. Demosthenes is gone. And if not by a Macedonian sword, but according to your own law, then grant him this, that I no longer exist, and grant yourselves this, that I did not fall at his hands, or, if you like, grant this at least to me as well. Surely I am worthy of this favour from you, especially since it is also possible to soothe him by an embassy, saying: 'The man you hated we have found a man of worth in our affairs, and we could not refrain from granting him this much. So forgive us if, dividing the matter, we honoured you by his death, and him by letting it suffice that it happen here, as against you,' especially when Demades also comes and pleads and persuades, a man who is your friend and intimate.

38. Since I am about to die, I will tell you, men of Athens, what grieves me and what gladdens me as I depart. I am glad that, though many combined against me and every day tried me, impeached me, indicted me, I live and take part in public life, and every accuser has gone away blushing; but I am pained that I could not console the parents of those who fell at Chaeronea as I wished. For I, fathers of noble sons, was considering how I might send [them] off now, how I might show more Macedonian dead and more prisoners, but evening, as you see, prevents me from doing this.

But you, at least, take my place for yourselves. Ease your mourning, and, since you have become fathers of the city's sons, this I beg, give dignity also to the speech that will be delivered over them. Elect as speaker one of those who truly grieve, not of those who pretend to. And when you have finished lamenting those good men, seek vengeance for what you have suffered: noble speeches, a fine decree, useful action.

40. Hyperides, Polyeuctus and Moerocles, let this affair concerning me make you no worse. But as long as it is allowed, pursue this dangerous statesmanship, for it is noble, even if it holds great dangers; and if you see envoys from Macedonia running after you on similar terms, forestall their speeches by death. And grant the city something more than I did: that no speeches about a surrender be made among the Athenians.

41. About my daughter, even if I give no charge, I am confident. I leave her many fathers, those here and those among the other peoples. For surely they did not crown her father only to neglect her. And why speak of individuals? The whole people will take care of her upbringing, her bridegroom, her marriage. And if she bears a son, the name Demosthenes will perhaps be given to him. If a grandson is born, may he, O gods, surpass his grandfather in fortune, and in all else be like him.

42. Is there anything left worth saying? Yes. The envoys must hear a few words before they leave. O servants of a tyrant who has prospered beyond his deserts, how great and splendid a hope you have missed! You thought you would take me from the people and lead me in chains through the agora, through Eleusis, through the Plataeans, through the Thebans, through the Phocians, through Thermopylae, through Larissa, exposing in me the character of the people; but you go away empty-handed, having seen the courage of an orator.

So report the truth to your master: that the people had not yet made clear what it would do, for it said it would consider, but Demosthenes, keeping his reputation from him, drank the hemlock and died. Let him know that he is at war with such men, to whom every disgrace is more frightening than death.
